blocks.text: [III, 345] It is asked why the Egyptians are compared with flies in these words of Es. VII, 18. The Lord shall hiss for the fly that is in the uttermost part of the rivers of Egypt; and various writers offer various answers. Jerome: But he calls the Egyptians flies because of the filth of idolatry and because they are an unwarlike people. Basil thinks the reference is to τὸ εὐτελὲς τῶν ἀντικειμένων [to euteles tōn antikeimenōn] [III, 346] δυνάμεων· μυῖα γάρ ἐστι ζῶον ἀπὸ κόπρου τὴν γένεσιν ἔχον, ὀχληρὸν τοῖς ἀνθρώποις γένος, καὶ μυσαρὸν ὂν, καὶ ἡ ζωὴ ὀχληρὰ, καὶ ὁ θάνατος βδελυκτὸς [dynameōn; myia gar esti zōon apo koprou tēn genesin echon, ochlēron tois anthrōpois genos, kai mysaron on, kai hē zōē ochlēra, kai ho thanatos bdelyktos], the worthlessness of the forces that are opposed to the Israelites: for the fly is generated from dung, and is a kind hostile and abominable to men, whose life is troublesome and whose death is loathsome. But Cyril asserts that the Egyptians are compared with flies διά τοι τὸ πλῆθος, καὶ τὸ μὴ λίαν εὔηχες τῆς φωνῆς [dia toi to plēthos, kai to mē lian euēches tēs phōnēs], because of their multitude and their discordant and uncouth speech, as though it were not so much speech as the buzzing of flies. The simplest course seems to be to refer it to multitude, with the Chaldee [col. 499] translator, whose paraphrase runs thus: יכלי יי לעם קטרי משרית גבריא דסגיאין כרבביא וייתינון מארעא דמצרים, The Lord shall call to the people of the bands of the army of mighty men (that is, in which forces of mighty men are joined together and sworn in league), who are many as flies, and he shall bring them from the land of Egypt. R. Selomo too understands here חילות רבות כזבובים, an army numerous like flies. And Abarbanel: המשיל אותם בזבוב לקלות מרוצתם ולרוב האספם, He compares them with flies because of the swiftness of their course and because of the multitude of their gathering. The former of these comes from Kimchi, the latter from the Chaldee and Solomon; I think the latter is to be preferred, because Egypt was once populous beyond belief. Herodotus, book 2, chapters 60 and 177, relates that seven hundred thousand people assembled at Bubastis for the festival of Diana, and that twenty thousand cities in Egypt were inhabited under Amasis. In the kingdom of Ptolemy Philadelphus, of which Egypt was the greatest part, Theocritus, Idyll 17, counts more than thirty-three thousand towns. Rightly, then, are the Egyptians, whose multitude is immense, compared with flies. Hence Plautus in the Truculentus, Act 1, Scene 1:
For now there are almost more pimps and harlots than there once were flies, when it is hottest.
And Homer, Iliad 2, line 469, says that the forces of the Greeks stood in great numbers in the Scamandrian meadow,
Ἠΰτε μυιάων ἁδινάων ἔθνεα πολλὰ [Ēute myiaōn hadinaōn ethnea polla], Like the very many tribes of thronging flies.
